Now, on Day 1, I gave my lecture and that went over really well. They took it well, as I largely pointed out that the odds were astronomically (truly) low. Given the span of the universe, the inherent limits of energy transfer, the time scales involved, our location in the observable universe, etc...

It's now when I should tell you that I was obnoxiously drunk - and kind of being an asshole. Like I said, they took it well.

On Day 1, after my talk, I was to open it up for a half hour for open questions. After explaining that I'm not a physicist, I proceeded to answer questions entirely about physics - sort of. The things they asked about... Well... "Can you prove that aliens aren't here?" "Can you prove that they can't harvest anti-matter and exceed the speed of light?" "Can you prove dark matter isn't going to enable them to reach us?" Things like that...

Most of the questions where about dark matter - which, I can assure you, we knew even less about then than we do now. And, yet, they thought it was everything from magic fairy dust to the eventual doom of humanity. We hadn't learned about dark energy - yet. Thankfully...

Then, I went and got even more drunk. See, I'd been paid $200 to give my talk. I also got plane fare, room, board, and a mother-fucking open bar! Yup... I had all the booze I could possibly want and then some! It was pretty awesome.

Day 2, I was on a panel of experts. These experts included authors, one guy from JPL, and some guy who makes documentaries. I don't think he has any qualifications and I'm pretty sure the guy at JPL was only there 'cause we sure as hell didn't want that bastard to be unemployed.

For two hours, I sat there and explained the math - over and over again, and the physics, of why it's so very improbable that we'd have met alien life and that we'd somehow managed to keep it a secret. This is confounded by my need to tell the truth. See, the truth is that alien life almost certainly exists. Intelligent alien life almost certainly exists, has existed, and will exist in the future.

Which gets me back to the dark matter... After the debate, which included a bunch of references to dark matter and how gravity is only a theory and the speed of light is only a theoretical physical limit, we had two hours of questions. I'd filled my water with vodka and my water container was also full of more booze.

By the end of it, I'm ranting and raging about how we're possibly all aliens and that the whole thing is a conspiracy - in other words, I'm mocking them. However, self-awareness doesn't seem to be a primary characteristic for ufologists and they thought they'd converted me to their side.

Basically, in public - in front of some 500 people, I made up wild theories about dark matter (note: I'm distinctly not a physicist - I'm a mathematician and hadn't even earned my Ph.D yet) and how it was all a government conspiracy. Fortunately, this was before YouTube was even a concern.

To top it off, I was invited back to the same function for the next few years. I declined to go - but I can only imagine what the alcohol bill cost them.

And that's my story about giving a presentation at a convention for ufologists. Yay! Academia!
